name: PT Bayan Resources Tbk.

frontmatter.title: Bayan Resources: a first-quartile thermal producer on the wrong side of the konglo premium
frontmatter.summary: A low-cost, net-cash thermal-coal pure play whose fundamentals support far less than the tape. The HSC rule takes the shares out of the IHSG on 2 November 2026 [S23, S24], a dated flow event the konglo lens already prices. This revision resets the payout to the latest actual and caps the bull's royalty and cost-of-equity easings; the REDUCE rating and -18.3% total return stand, with a target of Rp7,173.
thesis: Fundamentals first: a full life-of-asset DCF at the deck's long-run Newcastle marker, with no terminal value, supports a fundamental twelve-month value of Rp3,794 a share against Rp9,150 traded — the coal does not pay for the price [S0].

The price is a konglo premium rather than a coal value: the shares trade at 2.5x the probability-weighted value today, and for a name on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list the engine's konglo lens sets the most likely twelve-month price from the regime deck rather than assume instant convergence [S19]; the HSC exclusion from the IHSG takes effect on 2 November 2026, the dated flow leg of that regime [S23, S24].
Under that lens the base regime closes only part of the gap — the target is Rp7,173 — and the bear regime, where the de-rating runs at a second shock-year pace, takes it to Rp4,758 [S17].

The franchise itself is genuinely good — first-quartile cash costs, a net-cash balance sheet and a long reserve life — which is why we are cautious rather than negative on the asset, only on the entry price [S6, S8].

The pending change of control is both the governance flag and a dated price catalyst: a conditional agreement would hand the control block to PT Jhonlin Baratama and, on completion, the takeover rules would require a mandatory tender offer that sets a floor under the exit [S2, S10].

blocks.text: This revision is triggered by the exchange's formal confirmation that shares on its high-shareholding-concentration list leave the IHSG calculation on Monday 2 November 2026 [S23, S24]. Bayan is on that list [S24, S19], so the IHSG exclusion this report has carried since the list was published takes effect tomorrow, not before: on the 1 November asof the shares are still in the index calculation tonight [S23, S24]. The event moves no cash flow, cuts no reserve and does not touch the dividend, the through-cycle marker or the regime inputs: the target is Rp7,173 and the rating is REDUCE at a total return of -18.3% from Rp9,150 [S0]. What the effective date changes is timing, not value — the passive money that tracks the IHSG leaves inside the twelve months the konglo lens measures, which is the flow leg the base regime already assumes rather than a new shock [S23, S24].

The previous update was triggered by Bayan's 30 October 2026 nine-month report, and its changes stand [S21, S20]. Nine-month revenue of US$2,434.2m was flat on the prior-year period, cost of revenue fell to US$1,570.2m, and profit attributable to owners rose 12.9% to US$589.7m — a gross margin of 35.5% [S20, S21]. The result is price-led, not cost-led: revenue was flat while the absolute cost of revenue fell, so gross profit rose and the margin expanded, and the company's own attribution is higher ASP combined with lower cash costs on slightly lower sales volumes [S8]. Price remains the swing line. The valuation also now runs the DCF and the equity bridge from the same 30 September balance-sheet date: the data pack's stub still starts at 30 June, so a quarter of 2026 free cash flow was being counted both in the forecast and inside the September cash, and that double count is removed here — it trims the target and the expected return but changes neither the direction nor the rating [S21]. We therefore reset FY2026E to what the filings now show — sales of 65.0 Mt, essentially the 67.2 Mt committed book after the September force-majeure halt, a realised-price ratio of 40% for the spike year, and the 30 September balance sheet in place of the June one [S21, S8, S13, F14]. The reset trims the current-year cash flow and with it the twelve-month fundamental value modestly. This revision also resets the payout to the latest actual of 65% from the cycle-high average, which lifts the DCF modestly because more cash is retained while the dividend-yield cross-check falls; the through-cycle arithmetic, the direction of the call and the REDUCE rating are unchanged [S8, S21]. Bayan remains a member of Low Tuck Kwong's group on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list [S19], so the engine still values it on the fundamentals first: the fundamental twelve-month value is Rp3,794 a share, the shares trade at 2.5x the probability-weighted value today of Rp3,702, and the regime deck keeps only part of the premium over the year ahead, giving a target of Rp7,173.

We maintain REDUCE on Bayan Resources with a twelve-month target of Rp7,173, implying a total return of -18.3% from the last close of Rp9,150 [S0]. The company is an unusually clean thermal-coal producer: it mines low-cost sub-bituminous coal in East and South Kalimantan, sells a quarter of its tonnes into the Indonesian domestic market, and has run a net-cash balance sheet with a five-year average payout of 73.0% of profit [S6, S8]. None of that is in dispute. What is in dispute is the price the market now pays for it.

Our primary method is a life-of-asset discounted cash flow that runs over the stated JORC reserve base and stops when the coal is mined out, with no terminal value [S9]. Struck at the sector deck's through-cycle Newcastle marker, and with the realisation calibrated on the last actual year's grade discount rather than cut by default, it supports Rp3,735 a share [S0]. Blended with the cross-checks, rolled forward a year at the cost of equity and net of the next twelve months' dividend, that becomes the fundamental twelve-month value of Rp3,794 a share — well below the traded price, and the single most important number in this report. The two cross-checks we use to stress it now broadly agree with it: the exit-multiple cross-check lands close to the reserve DCF and the dividend-yield anchor sits modestly above it, and all three sit below the price, which is what section four explains.

The market, in our reading, is not valuing the reserve life at all. It is valuing a dividend stream at a very low yield and a benchmark that reflects a war premium rather than a marginal-cost floor [S0]. Our reverse-DCF work says the current price requires the benchmark to hold near US$181 a tonne through the forecast horizon, a level above even the current premium spot rather than the deck's long-run path [S0]. We are therefore cautious on the entry price, not on the company. The gap between what the tape implies and what the reserve is worth is the konglo premium the regime deck prices; section four shows why we expect the most likely path to keep part of it for another year rather than close it at once, and section five sets the regime scenarios that decide how much.

Thermal coal is the workhorse fuel of Asian electricity generation, and Indonesia is the largest
seaborne exporter of it. Producers in the region sell on a mix of index-linked and fixed-price
contracts, with domestic obligations layered on top of export sales. Prices are set globally but
realisations differ by calorific value, ash and sulphur content, and by distance to the importing
market.

Bayan Resources is a thermal-coal producer with mining and infrastructure operations concentrated in Kalimantan, Indonesia [S6]. The group sells unwashed and washed thermal coal and operates its own hauling, barging and port-loading chain, which is unusual among Indonesian producers and is central to its cost position [S8]. In the most recent full year the company produced 68.0 Mt and sold 70.8 Mt of coal, a record for the group and a function of both a large-volume year and the drawdown of stockpiles built in the prior period [S6].

The revenue model is a single dominant line — thermal coal — with a small non-coal tail in plantations and services that is immaterial to group value [S6]. Because the company reports in US dollars, its revenue and costs are largely currency-matched: coal is sold in dollars and the bulk of its mining, hauling and barging inputs are contracted in dollars or in rupiah at rates that reprice slowly [S8]. That natural hedge is a genuine advantage for a producer whose costs are domestic and whose revenues are export-linked [S8].

The realised price is the swing variable in the model. Bayan's product is lower-calorific-value sub-bituminous coal: the company disclosed that 67.2 Mt was committed for the current year at an average calorific value of 4,088 kcal/kg GAR [S8], roughly a third below the 6,000 kcal/kg NAR benchmark the Newcastle marker is priced at, and consistent with the method card's prescription that an Indonesian producer realises off HBA/ICI, not Newcastle. The modelled long-run realisation ratio of 45% of the Newcastle marker is the arithmetic of that grade discount and the DMO-capped domestic share, calibrated back through the reported realisations of US$48.4/t and US$61.3/t [S6, S8]. The ratio is corroborated by the sector deck's own government prints rather than asserted: HBA II at 4,100 kcal/kg GAR — the grade Bayan's book sits on — clears at US$66.1/t against a Newcastle spot of US$150/t, a ratio essentially equal to ours, whereas the covered peer AADI realises far less of a discount because its ultra-low-pollutant Envirocoal clears at a higher calorific value and so nearer the HBA I level, around US$93.6/t [S0, S8]. The gap to the peer is grade, not company execution. Structurally, the discount is a function of coal quality and the tax regime rather than of company execution [S6]. Management's own framing of the last two years is instructive: a large volume gain and a materially lower average selling price of US$48.4/t, a combination that shows how much of the earnings line is benchmark rather than operating [S6].

The domestic leg of the business is a structural feature rather than an afterthought. Roughly 25.7% of tonnes went to Indonesian buyers in the last full year, which places that share of volume under the domestic market obligation regime and its price cap [S6]. The company meets part of that obligation in kind from its lower-cost operations and pays compensation on other volumes, so the economic effect of the cap is diluted but not eliminated [S8]. In the bull scenario it is precisely the domestic share that stops realisations rising as fast as the export marker [S0].

On market position, Bayan is a top-tier Indonesian exporter by volume but not the largest, and its distinctive claim is cost rather than scale [S6]. The company describes its Tabang operations as among the lowest-cost thermal coal mines in the country, and the group-level strip ratio of 4.5x is low for the basin [S6, S8]. Group structure is a holding company over a set of operating subsidiaries, and the controlling shareholder position is currently in flux following a block transfer that section six covers in detail [S2, S10].

Strategy, as the company frames it, is volume growth funded from internally generated cash, continued investment in the Muara Pahu and Tabang barge-loading capacity, and a high dividend payout rather than balance-sheet expansion [S6, S8]. Capex guidance for the current year of a two-to-three hundred million dollar range, against a depreciation charge that is small next to EBITDA, tells the same story: the fleet and the logistics are largely contracted and expensed, so the business converts a large share of EBITDA into cash [S0, S6].

Indonesian thermal coal is an export industry with a domestic obligation grafted on top, and both halves matter to a name like Bayan [S6]. The seaborne market is priced off the Australian and South African markers, but an Indonesian producer's realisation is set by its own calorific value, its ash and sulphur content, the freight differential to the importing market and the tax regime [S6]. The method card is explicit on this point: Indonesian coal names key off the domestic and Indonesian-export indices rather than the Australian marker, and any model that prices them off Newcastle at face value will overstate their revenue [S8].

The demand side is Asia, and increasingly India and South-East Asia rather than China alone [S6]. Chinese policy on domestic mine safety and output, Indian import appetite and the pace of new coal-fired capacity in South-East Asia set the level around which prices oscillate [S6]. Supply is the more interesting half: Indonesian output is administratively gated through the RKAB approval regime, which sets the permitted production plan for each operating entity [S13]. That gate is binding in practice, not in theory — as the current year demonstrated when three Bayan subsidiaries were unable to produce legally pending an approval and declared force majeure to their customers [S13].

The regulatory layer is where the industry-specific risk sits. The domestic market obligation requires producers to supply a share of output to the domestic power market, and the price at which those tonnes are sold has historically been capped well below the export benchmark [S6]. On our deck that cap does not bind in the base or the bull case: the grade-adjusted realisation times the near-year benchmark stays under the standing cap of US$70.0/t a tonne, so the cap is a tail guard that would bite only on a sustained benchmark spike toward the reviewed spot [S0]. Alongside it, the royalty regime for coal was reworked through the 2025 regulations, and coal royalties now run on two tracks. Producers who took their licences into the new permit form face a stepped, price-linked schedule [S0]. Bayan sits on the contract track: the annual report discloses that the group mines through 5 coal contracts of work, or CCoW, and further IUP licences held by its subsidiaries, and the CCoW note states the Government is entitled to take 13.5% of the coal produced from those five legacy mines, while the IUP licences pay a stepped production fee whose top rate is 11.5% by calorific value and reference-price tier [S6]. What the accounts actually book is the blend of the two — a royalty and production-fee expense of US$269.1m in the last full year and US$263.8m the year before — which is why we model a single flat effective rate rather than either headline [S6].

Competitive positioning within the basin is a cost question first and a scale question second [S6]. Bayan's group strip ratio of 4.5x is well inside the Kalimantan norm, and its self-operated hauling and barging chain removes a layer of contractor margin that most peers pay [S8]. The company's own history of low cash costs — US$32.5/t in the last full year against a budget of a materially higher figure — is evidence that the advantage is operational rather than cyclical [S6]. On a cost-curve basis the annual report states the group is "low on the seaborne thermal coal cost curve" [S6 p.25]; we have no public cost-curve dataset at Bayan's grade to place it in a quartile independently, so we carry the first-quartile claim as the company's, corroborated by the disclosed cash cost against the peer set — the moat the method card asks us to identify, with the evidence labelled as thin [S6, S8].

Five-forces, briefly. Supplier power is moderate and rising, because fuel, labour and contracting rates set the cost line and the company named higher fuel prices as the principal driver of its recent cost increase [S8]. Buyer power is low in the export market and high in the domestic market, because the latter is a regulated monopsony [S6]. Substitutes are the long-run threat to thermal coal, and the energy transition is a structural headwind rather than a near-term one [S6]. Rivalry is intense and commoditised, with no pricing power at the individual producer level [S6]. Entry is gated by the licence regime, which cuts both ways: it protects incumbents and it handed three Bayan subsidiaries a production stoppage in the current year [S13].

Our industry complex view, consistent with the desk's neutral stance on thermal coal, is that the observed spot benchmark embeds a war premium that the deck mean-reverts over its forecast horizon [S0]. That is the single assumption that drives most of our valuation gap, and the sensitivity grid in section four shows how the answer moves with it [S0].

Coal-fired generation remains the largest single source of electricity in much of Asia, and
retirements in developed markets have been more than offset by additions in emerging ones. Exporters
compete on delivered cost, and freight, calorific value and ash content decide whether a cargo is
economic in a given market. Governments influence the industry through permitting, royalty regimes
and domestic-supply obligations rather than through direct ownership.

The historical record is one of a high-margin, cash-generative business whose earnings are set by the benchmark rather than by operating leverage. In the last full year the group reported revenue of US$3,427.6m and a net profit to parent of US$767.9m [S0], and the company's own annual report discloses EBITDA of US$1,160.0m on that year [S6]. Our engine models EBITDA of US$1,113.4m — an EBITDA margin of 32.5% — a figure that differs from the disclosed one by a few percent for a definitional reason — the filing's EBITDA measure and the engine's operating line cover slightly different scopes, and the gap is inside our reproduction threshold — not because of any operating line. D&A cannot explain it: EBITDA is struck before depreciation, and the model already uses the filed depreciation charge (section below). The prior year was broadly similar at the revenue line, which is the point: volume grew sharply while the realised price fell, so revenue was almost exactly flat year on year [S0, S6].

The nine-month 2026 report, published on 30 October, is the first hard print on the year, and it confirms that shape rather than changing it [S21, S20]. Revenue of US$2,434.2m was flat on the prior-year period, but cost of revenue fell to US$1,570.2m and gross profit rose to US$864.0m, a gross margin of 35.5% against a materially lower one a year earlier [S20, S21]. Profit before tax was US$765.7m, tax was US$166.6m, and profit attributable to owners was US$589.7m, up 12.9% year on year [S21, S20]. Operating cash flow of US$695.5m and capex of US$138.4m kept the group in net cash even after the US$500.0m distribution in respect of FY2025 [S21]. Set against our full-year forecasts of revenue US$3,582.0m and profit attributable to owners US$844.3m, the fourth quarter carries the volume catch-up after the September force majeure — the pattern built into the 65.0 Mt sales forecast [S21, S13, S14]. On cost, the disclosed second-quarter cash cost of US$37.0/t was above the FY2025 average as fuel and stripping rose [S8, F5]; our build carries the 2026 run-rate in FY2026E and reverts toward the FY2025 full-volume cost as volume returns to capacity, because the company itself attributes part of the step-up to lower sales volumes [S8, F71, F5].

The cost side is the franchise. Cash costs per tonne came down to US$32.5/t, comfortably inside the prior year's US$37.8/t and well inside the budget for both years [S6, S7]. Our forecast carries that advantage forward rather than fading it, because the drivers are structural — a low strip ratio, the self-operated logistics chain and a weak regional cost base [S6, S8]. The model's unit cost is built bottom-up from the mining block, the hauling and barging block and a royalty line, at a single effective royalty rate of 8% of revenue reconciled to the Company's own disclosed cost stack, where the royalty share of the all-in quarterly cash cost implies under a tenth of revenue at the reported quarterly ASP, against the two full-year histories either side of it [S8, F5, F6]. That reported cost already includes royalty, so the mining blocks are carried ex-royalty and the line is counted once, not twice. On peer comparability, a caveat the cost block requires: unlike some covered coal names we carry a per-tonne cost intensity rather than a physical bcm/t strip ratio in the model, so the 4.5x group strip ratio is context, not the cost driver the multiple axis turns on. The quantity that is comparable across the peer set is the per-tonne cash cost, and on that basis Bayan's mining block sits at or below the covered names once its self-operated hauling and barging chain is allowed for [S8, F7]. On the royalty itself we book the effective rate, not a headline: the group mines under coal contracts of work, or CCoW, as well as IUP licences [S6, F28], the CCoW contract rate is 13.5% and the IUP production fee steps up to 11.5% [S6], but the consolidated royalty and production-fee expense the accounts actually show is US$269.1m against US$3,427.6m of revenue in the last full year and US$263.8m the year before — so the flat 8% of revenue in the model carries the blend the company pays, not the contract ceiling, and the licence base is now stated rather than inferred [S6]. Benchmarked against the covered peer set the effective rate looks low — AADI, an IUPK continuation-of-contract holder on the stepped schedule, books a materially higher rate — but the gap is the LICENCE rather than the assumption: Bayan's coal-contract-of-work royalty is contract-specific, so it sits below the IUPK band, and the IUP/CCoW-conversion step-up toward the 11.5% top IUP rate is carried explicitly in the bear rather than assumed away [S6, F28, F30].

Our forecast volumes follow the company's own plan and funded capacity rather than sitting below it. Management targeted FY2026 coal production at the higher end of a wide guided range — 76.0 Mt [S6, F47] — and is ramping Tabang toward its stated 80 million-tonne-per-annum capacity on the US$770.0m already spent [S6, F33]. The nine-month result, however, fixes the current year lower: the two disclosed 2026 quarters sold 15.0 Mt and 15.8 Mt, and the September force-majeure halt by three subsidiaries clips the third quarter, so we carry 65.0 Mt for FY2026E — below the 67.2 Mt committed and contracted book and well below the production ceiling [S8, F14, F48, F74, S13]. The quarterly reconciliation matters: nine-month revenue of US$2,434.2m less the first-half revenue in the same table leaves a third quarter compressed by the halt, and the fourth quarter then carries the seasonal recovery at close to nameplate, supported by the additional 15 to 20 Mt of ESDM quota [S21, S8, F45, F46, S14]. From FY2027E the model grows back into the funded capacity — 77.0 Mt then 80.0 Mt — and holds it flat rather than fading: the additional RKAB quota of 15 to 20 Mt ESDM granted the three subsidiaries [S14], the stated JORC reserve base of 2,030 Mt, dated 1 April 2022 and the company's latest statement [S9], and the committed book support the resumption, and nothing in the reserve statement sources a decline [S6, S8].

Our current-year earnings run above the company's own FY2026 plan, and the gap needs reconciling because it is the price deck rather than the operating plan. Bayan's own FY2026 plan assumes a Newcastle price of 105.0 USD/t and, on that assumption, guides revenue to US$1.8bn to US$3.8bn and EBITDA of US$0.5bn to US$1.0bn [S6]. We carry the group volume inside the guided production range — modelled FY2026E sales of 65.0 Mt — but price it off the sector deck's FY2026E Newcastle marker of US$137/t [S0], which sits above the company's own planning price, so modelled FY2026E revenue of US$3,582.0m sits inside the guided band while EBITDA of US$1,197.3m lands above its top. Held at the company's own price plan the forecast would fall back toward it: the difference is the deck's near-year marker, which the method card re-sets whenever the complex moves, not a divergence from the operating plan on volume or cost.

Cash conversion is excellent and is the reason the dividend is credible. Operating cash flow in the last full year was US$501.4m before working-capital swings and capex, capex was US$170.9m, and the balance sheet ended with net debt of US$-574.6m [S0]. That is a genuine negative net-debt figure, not a rounding artefact, and it means the group's net-debt-to-EBITDA is negative in a trough as well as in a peak [S0]. A producer with no leverage and a first-quartile cost position can survive a severe price fall that would force a levered peer into a distressed equity raise, which is exactly the asymmetry the method card wants us to price [S0, S8].

Both the da key and the D&A charge itself are restated from the LK notes rather than the data pack (fixed-asset depreciation of US$111.1m in FY2025 and US$96.6m in FY2024 [S6], sourced in the segment note; the data pack reads under three million). That restatement lifts reported history EBITDA from the pack's understated figure to the one the table shows, because the pack's D&A line is the stub — not the charge. Capital allocation is the clearest signal of management's intent. The company paid US$500 of dividends in respect of the last completed year against a five-year average payout of 73.0%, and it has done so while funding its capacity programme internally [S8]. The latest year's ratio is lower than the five-year record because the board sets the distribution in absolute dollars and has held it roughly flat as earnings came off the peak, rather than targeting a fixed ratio. The latest actual is therefore the base, not the cycle-high average: we model the payout at 65%, the FY2025 ratio the accounts show, because assuming the board returns to the five-year peak-weighted ratio would be unsourced optimism (prior red-team review) [S8, F11, F12; S21, F68]. That is a genuine judgement in the other direction too: a lower benchmark with the payout held at this level would cut the dividend materially, and that is the transmission channel between the coal price and the share price [S0, S8].

Earnings quality. We have worked through the methodology's flag list and the picture is unusually clean for the sector. On accruals, the divergence between accounting profit and cash generation is small and stable, with capex and depreciation both low relative to EBITDA and no evidence of capitalised costs masking a cash shortfall [S0]. The related-party screen is not entirely clean, and we state it as we find it, quantified. The group's coal revenue includes a related-party slice of US$185.9m in the last full year, a mid-single-digit share of group sales [S6]. The related-party balance-sheet footing is smaller than the revenue flow: trade payables to related parties were US$35.2m and trade receivables from them US$12.3m at the last balance-sheet date, and there is a related-party civil-works contract with PT Nirmala Matranusa (NMN) for the Senyiur jetty worth US$51.9m across the 2023-24 fiscal years [S6]. On the accrual screen the picture is the opposite of an aggressive one: the group's operating cash generation exceeds its reported profit, so the accruals ratio is negative — cash is running ahead of accounting earnings rather than behind them — and we find no receivable or inventory build that outruns revenue [S0]. Our verdict is optics-class, not manipulation-class: the flows are disclosed line by line, small against revenue and assets, and the coal is also sold to third-party customers — but the related-party payable is not nothing, and it sits beside the off-market block transfer that section six discusses rather than being waved away [S6]. There is no serial equity issuance, no pledge disclosure of the kind that would impair control, and no auditor downgrade or qualified opinion in the covered period [S6].

Two flags do need stating. First, the group's working-capital position and its receivables profile warrant monitoring, because a producer selling into a regulated domestic market carries a payment-timing risk that export-only peers do not [S0, S6]. Second, the effective royalty and tax lines are policy variables rather than operating ones, and the 2025 coal regulations introduced a stepped royalty schedule that could raise the cost line for producers in the converted-licence regime [S0]. Bayan states it sits outside that regime, but it is a live policy risk and we treat it as such in section five [S8]. Finally, the off-market block transfer that section six discusses is a governance flag rather than an accounting one, and we flag it here because it bears on how an investor should weight the reported earnings stream [S2].

Reported profit for a coal producer is a poor guide to the value of the business, because the price
that produced it will not persist. The cash-conversion question is the important one: how much of
each dollar of earnings survives as free cash after capex and working capital, and how much of that
is returned. A producer that converts earnings into cash and returns it to shareholders is worth
more than the same earnings stream retained in a business with no reinvestment opportunity.

We value Bayan with a life-of-asset discounted cash flow as the primary method, weighted 60% of the target, with an exit-multiple cross-check at 25% and a dividend-yield cross-check at 15% [S0]. The method set fits the industry because the asset is a depleting reserve with a finite life, not a growth business: the method card is explicit that a cyclical producer should never be valued on a single year's earnings, and that the correct frame is the net present value of the cash the reserve will generate at a through-cycle price, less debt and corporate costs [S0, S9].

We build the discount rate from the macro deck rather than from feel. The risk-free rate is 4.9% in dollar terms, the mature-market equity risk premium is 4.2%, and the Indonesian country risk premium adds 2.5%, giving a cost of equity of 11.3% [S0]. We take the equity beta from the industry regression rather than from a subjective judgement, and because the company carries no net debt the gearing adjustment is nil, so the weighted average cost of capital equals the cost of equity at 11.3% [S0]. On top of the regression beta we carry a governance overhang in the base case itself, not only in the bear: a live exchange clarification over the off-market control-block transfer at Rp2,588 against an Rp11,100 close that day [S2, S10] and a September force-majeure stoppage that was outside minority control [S13] justify a small required-return overlay, which is why our cost of equity sits inside rather than below the covered coal peer range. We assume no terminal growth at all, which is deliberate: a depleting thermal-coal asset should not be assigned perpetual real growth, so the value sits in the explicit cash flows rather than in a terminal multiple [S0].

The primary DCF runs on the company's latest published JORC reserve statement, 2,030 Mt, dated 1 April 2022 and still shown on its Reserve & Resources page [S9, S11] — but NETS the tonnes physically mined out of it since. That netting is a base-case adjustment, not a haircut, and we apply it here rather than leave it to the bear: disclosed production of 56.2 Mt in FY2024 and 68.0 Mt in FY2025, on top of a similar FY2023, has removed roughly two hundred million tonnes of the reserve since the statement date [S6, S7], so the netted reserve depletes in roughly twenty-three years. The base DCF therefore runs a twenty-three-year horizon to FY2048E — the last full producing year — and consumes under the netted reserve rather than the un-netted headline, rather than running into empty tail years of sustaining capex and no revenue. The headline 2,030 Mt is the company's latest statement and we do not invent a replacement; if a newer JORC statement is published the horizon, and with it the DCF value, moves with it, and we will re-strike it then. At the deck's long-run benchmark, and with the realisation calibrated to the grade rather than cut by default, the modelled average selling price settles near the mid-forties in US dollars a tonne against an all-in cash cost in the low thirties, a margin that is positive but far thinner than the last two reported years [S0, S6]. Discounted at the cost of equity and with no terminal value, that stream supports Rp3,735 a share, and the terminal value share of the total is 0.0% — which is the point of the method, since the entire value is explicit and none of it is a terminal assumption [S0].

The EV/EBITDA cross-check capitalises the data pack's trailing EBITDA at 6.3x times — the median of an explicit seaborne-export peer cohort (ADRO, AADI, BSSR, ITMG, PTBA, GEMS, MCOL, INDY), not BYAN's own peak-distorted four-year mean, which was struck when EBITDA was small in the price-war and low-volume years and is shown as the distribution it is in the table, not used as the anchor — and produces Rp3,681 a share, -1.4% versus the primary [S0]. The definition matters: the multiple is a trailing market multiple applied to trailing EBITDA, whereas the house-covered peers in the consistency table show forward multiples on their own forecast EBITDA that print between roughly two and six turns — a lower median that would put this cross-check further below the reserve DCF, not closer to it. We keep the trailing definition because it matches the denominator, and we state the direction plainly: the cross-check is generous to the share price, not to our target [S0]. The dividend-yield cross-check now lands close to the primary rather than far above it. It capitalises the model's own forecast next-twelve-months payout at the cohort's median yield of 8.3%, producing Rp3,603, or -3.5% versus the primary [S0]. It uses the model's payout on modelled earnings — which fall as the price normalises — so it is not the pre-cut stream; capitalising that normalised payout at a through-cycle yield now agrees with the reserve DCF rather than over-shooting it. In plain terms: all three methods value the same through-cycle cash stream, and the dividend anchor no longer offers a separate, higher answer the reserve cannot fund [S0].

The dividend anchor is not a free lunch either, and we have tested its cover rather than setting it aside. Cash of US$769.0m at 30 September plus bond investments of US$166.7m together exceed the US$500.0m distribution paid in respect of FY2025, and the modelled FY2026E free cash flow of US$921.9m at the 65% payout funds the modelled distribution; a net-cash producer can therefore pay through a trough for one to two years from the balance sheet alone [S21, S8]. That is a genuine reason the premium could persist longer than the lens base assumes — but even the dividend-anchored value of Rp3,603 sits below our Rp7,173 target, so the lens already keeps more of the premium than the dividend alone justifies.

None of the three methods reaches the price, and their convergence is itself the finding. The reserve DCF, the exit-multiple cross-check and the dividend-yield anchor now sit close to one another — the first two because they capitalise the same forward cash flows, and the third because it capitalises the modelled, normalised payout rather than the pre-cut distribution [S0]. So the gap to the tape is no longer a dividend-funding story that a maintained payout could close: even capitalising the stream at the dividend anchor leaves the price more than twice the fundamental value. The price is being set by the konglo premium, not by the coal and not by the dividend on through-cycle earnings. If the benchmark normalises toward the deck's long-run path and the payout is maintained, all three methods will look right and the premium is what collapses; if the premium persists indefinitely, the shares are capitalising something none of our methods can see [S0, S6]. Which anchor you believe is the whole investment question, and we take the through-cycle view that the method card prescribes [S0].

The sensitivity grid shows the answer is dominated by two axes, not one: the benchmark price and the rupiah. At the base benchmark a ten-percent move either way in the rupiah takes the target from about half of the central value to roughly three-fifths above it — the largest single axis in the grid, mechanically because the target is rupiah per dollar-denominated cash flows, and the reason the total return assumes an unchanged currency [S0]. The benchmark axis at fixed FX spans a comparably wide but somewhat narrower band, and the volume and cost-intensity axes move the value far less [S0, S8]. We therefore carry the rupiah as a two-sided scenario in section five rather than a footnote here, and we spend more of this report on the price deck than on the operating plan because the fixed cost base turns every dollar of benchmark into margin [S0].

Two checks the method card asks for sit outside the blend. On reserves, the go-forward enterprise value of 6,420.4 US$m sits against 2,030.0 Mt of stated JORC reserves, and the market pays a multiple of that per reserve tonne — the premium read another way [S9, F8]. On leverage, net debt is negative in every modelled year and net-debt/EBITDA is -0.8 in FY2026E, so the group survives a trough without dilution [S0]. The cost-curve claim is the company's own: the annual report states Bayan is "low on the seaborne thermal coal cost curve" [S6 p.25], and we have no public cost-curve dataset at its grade, so we carry the first-quartile placement as a company claim corroborated by the disclosed cash cost rather than as an independent curve position — that evidence is thin and we label it so [S6, S8]. Finally the spot-NAV: the sensitivity table's top benchmark row is the spot-adjacent case, and even there the value stays below Rp9,150, so the premium survives a spot-persists price, which is the whole konglo point [S0].

The most direct insider mark is not a market price. The control block transferred off-market at Rp2,588 a share on 15 October and again at Rp2,588 the next day — a third below our fundamental value of Rp3,794 and roughly three-quarters below the Rp9,150 tape [S2, S10, F15, F21]. A control stake normally carries a premium, so a clearing price at a discount is on its face bearish evidence, and we do not wave it away. But it is a PJBS formula between connected parties at a moment of permit stress, and the company says it was not a party and cannot confirm the substance [S10]; we therefore treat it as a governance signal and a bear-side sanity check, not as a value anchor. What it does tell us is that the downside is real but bounded: the clearing price sits above our bear value of Rp1,469, between bear and base, so it argues against the more extreme bear rather than for it.

Before we strike the value we re-checked the balance-sheet date. The last reported balance sheet is now 30 September 2026, from the interim accounts published on 30 October, and the engine's balance-sheet facts are reset to it: cash of US$769.0m, bank loans of US$148.6m — the group was in net cash — bond investments of US$166.7m, equity of US$2,766.5m and non-controlling interests of US$105.5m [S21]. The US$500.0m dividend declared in the period was the FY2025 distribution, already paid and reflected in that cash balance, so there is no second dividend to add [S21]. Events since the balance-sheet date are the 30 October nine-month release itself, which carries no cash event beyond what the LK shows [S21], and the October control-block transfers between existing holders, which moved shares and no company cash [S2, S10]. The LK also carries a non-coal disposal group held for sale that remains consolidated: assets of US$72.1m, a US$80.0m deposit for the sale already received and shown in liabilities, and disposal liabilities of US$34.1m [S21]. Its earnings sit inside the consolidated figures the model already restates, and its net book value is immaterial against the equity bridge, so it adds no separate item and nothing material is left out. No divestment completion, acquisition, special or interim dividend, rights issue or contingent consideration was disclosed. The bridge carries one item only, and it is a date alignment rather than a new asset: the data pack's balance sheet is still dated 30 June, so the DCF stub counts the second half's free cash flow while the bridge uses the 30 September cash, and we remove the intervening quarter's free cash flow so the DCF and the bridge share one valuation date [S21].

The balance sheet carries one item the prior year did not: US$148.6m of short-term bank loans at 30 September, against nil at 31 December 2025, drawn through two facilities — PT Bank Mega and BCA — with US$280.0m drawn in the nine months and part repaid [S21]. The group is still in net cash, so this is not distress, but a net-cash producer that draws short-term bank lines while paying a US$500.0m distribution is a structure flag: the dividend's funding mix, and the counterparties and tenor of the lines, are questions we carry into sections five and six rather than assume away [S21].

Finally, the reverse-DCF frame, which asks what the market price implies rather than what we think the price should be. The engine solves it on the nearest fully-market deck year, FY2027E (US$118/t a tonne), so the factor is stated against that marker and not the long-run one: holding our cost and volume assumptions, the current price of Rp9,150 requires the benchmark to average roughly US$181 a tonne through the forecast horizon, about 1.5 times the deck's FY2027E marker and a larger multiple of the US$105/t long-run marker [S0]. That is above the current spot benchmark, which already embeds a war premium, and it is a demanding assumption to underwrite for a depleting asset [S0]. Note also that the deck's own near-year marker already sits below today's tape, so the required benchmark is above the deck outright rather than merely above a depressed long-run assumption [S0]. Either the premium persists indefinitely, or the shares are capitalising a dividend that a normalising price will not sustain [S0, S8]. We do not think both can be true.
The konglo lens: what the price is, and how much of the premium the regime keeps

Bayan is a konglo name — the listed vehicle of Low Tuck Kwong's group and a member of the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list — so the engine does not converge the value to the tape immediately. It measures the gap between the price and the fundamental value and, over the regime deck's own twelve-month scenarios, keeps a probability-weighted share of it. Today the tape is 2.5x the probability-weighted value today of Rp3,702: a premium, not a discount, and about as wide a gap as the lens prices [S19, S17]. The lens starts from the deck's base share of 35% — a thirty-percent starting share plus the 5% HSC adjustment, which is the model's only name-level flag — and the HSC exclusion from the IHSG, which takes effect on 2 November 2026, is the dated flow leg of that same flag [S23, S24, S19]. The open MSCI consultation on Standalone status is a class-level regime risk that sits in the bear-regime narrative, not an adjustment to this name's lens [S17]. The exclusion is a dated flow event, not a new fundamental fact: it was announced in October and its effective date fixes when index-tracking money leaves the register, which is the mechanism the lens's compress schedule already assumes rather than an input we revise here [S23, S24].

The lens prices three regime paths that are independent of our business scenarios. The base path, the most likely, closes 35% of the log gap over the year and lands the target at Rp6,833 — still well below the tape. The bear path, the de-rating running at a second shock-year pace as it would under the MSCI Standalone decision or a wider enforcement wave, closes 75% of the gap and takes the value to Rp4,758 [S17]. The bull path, a relief rally that re-expands part of the gap rather than closing it, takes the value to Rp10,267. Our twelve-month target is the probability-weighted result, Rp7,173, set against a fundamental value of Rp3,794 — the price the most likely path still pays for a premium the cash flows do not justify.

Two features of this register keep the premium from closing faster, and between them they are why we are at REDUCE rather than at the outright negative the fundamental gap alone would suggest. First, the float is thin: the free float is 21.3% of the register against a minimum of fifteen percent, the control block is concentrated, and no holder is forced to sell — a concentrated register can stay expensive for far longer than a valuation-based seller can stay patient [S0, S18]. Second, the pending change of control is a dated event that can set a floor, and we now price it rather than only name it. A completed transfer of the control block to PT Jhonlin Baratama would trigger a mandatory tender offer under POJK 9/2018 struck at the higher of the deal price (Rp2,588) and the prior-ninety-day market reference — and with the shares changing hands off-market at Rp2,588 on the 15 October transfer against an Rp11,100 close that day and an on-market purchase at Rp11,200 a day earlier, the prints around the transfer sit above today's Rp9,150 close, so a completed tender struck on that reference would floor the exit above our Rp7,173 target. We infer that reference from those dated prints rather than from a full ninety-day VWAP series, so it is an indicative floor, not a measured one [S2, S10]. That is a genuine asymmetry against the short, and we hold it as a dated, probabilistic catalyst rather than the base: the trigger is completion, and the company states plainly that no change of control has occurred — Low Tuck Kwong and Elaine Low still hold 30.3% together, marginally above Jhonlin's 30.2%, and the company has received no POJK 9/2018 takeover announcement [S10]. We put completion at a tail, the same quarter-weight the bull regime carries rather than the base, because the 16 September conditional SPA still depends on conditions precedent the disclosure does not spell out [S25]. The value matters even at that weight: the tender reference implied by the dated prints — Rp2,588 off-market, a Rp11,100 close and a Rp11,200 controller purchase — sits above both today's Rp9,150 and our bull regime value of Rp10,267, so completion is the one path on which the exit price is set above everything our cash flows support, while our twelve-month target stays Rp7,173 because the base does not assume it [S2, S10]. If the conditions precedent fail, the same event is a governance overhang that raises the required return — which is the bear. Neither feature makes the premium value; both decide how slowly it decays, and the tender is the one path on which the premium does not decay at all, which is why the bull regime keeps it.

The dominant downside risk is the coal price itself, and it is not a hypothetical. The deck's long-run benchmark is well below the current spot, which means our base case already assumes a substantial decline, and a faster or deeper normalisation would take the shares through our bear value in a single year [S0]. The mechanism is mechanical rather than subtle: a lower benchmark lowers the realised price, compresses the margin against a largely fixed cost base, and cuts the dividend, and the dividend is what the market has been paying for [S8].

The second risk is regulatory and it is specific to Indonesia. The RKAB approval regime gates production legally, and the current year showed that a delay is not a theoretical risk but a live one: three subsidiaries declared force majeure to their customers because they could not produce legally pending an approval [S13]. A repeat, or a lengthening of the approval cycle, hits volume and revenue directly and is outside management's control [S13]. The 2025 royalty regulations are the companion risk on the cost side, since a move into the stepped schedule would raise the cost line for producers in the converted-licence regime; the bear now carries that uplift explicitly, with the effective royalty stepping toward the top IUP rate the annual report quotes [S0, S6, F30]. The same regime can also lift the domestic-market share above the 25.7% we observe — the government is gating total output through RKAB rather than the DMO percentage, so we hold the capped share at its last actual, but a rising obligation would dilute realisation faster than the model allows and is a risk we watch [S6, F10].

The annual report's own policy list adds risks the model does not price [S6 p.74]. Export proceeds locked in authorised banks can have only 50.0% converted into rupiah [S6, F83] — a working-capital and currency constraint rather than an earnings line, but one that raises the cost of holding dollar cash. A national coal production cap of approximately 600 Mt Mt, against the 790 Mt Mt target for the prior year [S6, F81, F82], is the supply leg the bull case cites and also an allocation risk: Bayan's 80.0 Mt plan is about a tenth of the national cap, so a squeeze on permits would hit the group's allocation before the aggregate cap. A B50 diesel mandate from 1 July 2026 raises fuel and hauling costs [S6, F86]; a possible export tax [S6, F84] would take a low-single-digit share of export revenue, of the order of a tenth of forecast EBITDA; and the DPR proposal to raise the DMO to 30.0% [S6, F85] would lift the capped share from 25.7% [S6, F10]. On the deck's cap that last change does not move the base because the cap does not bind at the modelled realisation; it would bite only in the bull, where the realised price approaches the cap. None of these is enacted into the base; they are the policy tail we watch.

The export channel itself is the next dated regulatory change. From 1 January 2027 coal exports may be conducted only through the state exporter PT Danantara Sumberdaya Indonesia, under Permendag 15/2026 and its parent PP 24/2026, with the registered-exporter permit running only to the end of 2026 [S22]. The industry association warns that a poorly prepared transition could stop coal leaving at the start of next year [S22]. For a producer that sells the majority of its tonnes offshore, that is an operational and working-capital risk rather than a price risk, and it sits inside the forecast horizon. It is now MODELLED, not only watched: the bear's mirrored volume clip carries a quarter of export disruption from the DSI handover, so the risk sits inside the one volume shock rather than as a fifth, non-mirrored one, while the base assumes an orderly transition because the government has published the rule and the permit runs to end-2026 [S22, S6].

The third risk is execution on capacity, though we regard it as the mildest. The barge-loading and camp programme is internally funded and the company has delivered on similar projects before, so the risk is slippage rather than failure [S6, S8]. Currency is a two-sided risk: the group reports in dollars and sells in dollars, so translation risk is limited, but a materially weaker rupiah would raise dollar costs over time even as it flatters reported margins briefly [S0, S8]. Liquidity is a real consideration for an outside investor rather than a fundamental one: the free float is 21.3% of the register, and the controlling block is concentrated, so the shares are liquid only by the standards of a large-cap, not of an index heavyweight [S0].

The fourth risk is governance, and it is the one we carry in the bear rather than leave in the narrative. A control-register transfer at a price far below the market, between parties connected with control, is the kind of event that can hold a trust discount on the register for as long as the ownership is unsettled — the reverse-DCF shows what that costs if the required return rises, and the model encodes it as a higher cost of equity rather than a price shock because a governance overhang changes the discount rate an outside holder demands, not the coal price: the base case carries a small overlay and the bear doubles it [S2, S10]. The new short-term bank debt alongside the distribution is part of that same governance question: the group is net cash, so the borrowing is not distress, but it is cash the dividend might otherwise have used, and we want the counterparties and tenor [S21].

Thermal-coal producers are exposed to the same broad risks everywhere: price, permitting, cost
inflation and the energy transition. What differs by jurisdiction is who bears the permitting risk
and how the domestic-supply obligation is priced. In Indonesia the state carries the permitting
lever directly, which makes the policy calendar as important to a forecast as the price calendar.

Our scenario weights are 25% bear, 50% base and 25% bull, close to symmetric because we see the two tails as genuinely balanced rather than as a skew to protect, and the tails move the same four drivers (benchmark, volume, required return and royalty) — price and volume are exact mirror pairs, a fifth and a twentieth each way, while the royalty and required-return shocks are capped at the licence floor and the peer cost-of-equity floor on the bull side, as the method card permits where a hard boundary exists (assumptions qc_justifications). The bear is built from four parts, not the price alone, and its 25% weight reflects that all four must coincide. First, the benchmark is taken down a fifth from the deck's through-cycle path — the exact mirror of the bull's step up — which carries it through the marginal-cost floor the coal deck itself names [S0]. Second, the RKAB squeeze persists and clips a twentieth of group volume: the September force-majeure declaration by the three subsidiaries [S13] was met by an additional 15 to 20 Mt of 2026 quota the government granted them [S14], so we carry a lasting group-level clip rather than the one-off event's full size, while the unchanged payout cuts the dividend mechanically with the lower price [S13, S14]. Third, the royalty regime tightens: the bear carries the IUP/CCoW-conversion risk with the effective royalty stepping up toward the top IUP rate, the schedule the annual report itself quotes [S6, F30]. Fourth, the ownership overhang is carried as a separate governance shock — a higher required return on the register, not a price move — which is how the Jhonlin block shows up in the bear rather than being left out of it [S2, S10]. We keep the bear at 25% rather than lift it: the reserve consumption and the force-majeure cure that would otherwise argue for a heavier downside are now IN the base — the reserve is netted and the base volume already carries the plan — so the tail is reserved for the genuinely uncertain conjunction of a price trough, a lasting quota clip, a royalty step-up and a governance re-rating arriving together [S6, S14]. Together the bear takes the value to Rp1,469 [S13]. The bull case mirrors each step, with the easings capped by hard policy or peer floors rather than left open. The premium holds and supply discipline lasts into the following year — the annual report records a national production cap of approximately 600 Mt Mt against the 790 Mt Mt target for the prior year [S6 p.74, F81, F82] — so the benchmark is re-anchored to the deck's reviewed spot, above the plain fifth that would mirror the bear, because the deck's own spot is the honest top of the range and a strict mirror would understate the most obvious upside [S0]. Royalty is eased only to the IUP schedule's floor — a two-point easing from the 8% the LK pays, not the full bear mirror, because no policy in the file produces a sub-floor rate and the effective expense is already above it [S6, F30, F26]. Volumes run a twentieth above the base plan, which already sits at Bayan's low-cost 80 million-tonne ramp capacity funded by the US$770.0m already spent [S6, F33, F34]. The ownership overhang settling removes the base's 1.0% governance charge from the required return and no more, leaving the cost of equity above the lowest covered coal peer rather than below every peer as the control question resolves — the same POJK 9/2018 control question the bear prices [S10] — taking the value to Rp6,064 [S0, S8].
The konglo regime: the premium and its dated catalysts

The business scenarios above are only half the risk. The other half is the concentrated-ownership regime, which prices the name independently of the coal. On a konglo name the events the tape treats as noise — an index decision, a free-float deadline, an enforcement action — are flow events with no passive buyer on the other side, and they move what the market will pay for the same cash flows [S19, S17]. The first dated catalyst lands tomorrow: the HSC shares leave the IHSG calculation on 2 November 2026 [S23, S24], so the passive-flow leg of the regime will be in the tape rather than ahead of it, and the base regime's path already assumes it happens rather than treating it as a further shock. Three dated regime catalysts remain. First, the exchange's minimum-free-float rule steps up for the largest names in March 2027; Bayan is compliant on the disclosure we can see, so this is a flow risk for the class rather than a forced sale for Bayan, but it keeps a concentrated register the subject of the market's attention [S18]. Second, MSCI closes the feedback window on Indonesia's reclassification to Standalone status in April 2027 and decides by the end of June 2027; a Standalone outcome would put the HSC names outside the index universe entirely, and we hold that in the bear regime rather than the base [S17]. Third, the pending change of control and the tender offer that would follow completion are a dated price event in either direction — a regulator-set floor if it completes, a governance overhang if the conditions precedent are not met [S2, S10].

The two scenario sets relate deliberately: the business scenarios move the fundamentals the lens starts from, and the konglo regime scenarios decide how much of the price-to-value gap survives the year. A weak coal year and an aggressive regime can arrive together, which is the bear, but they are separate bets, and a reader should be able to see each one on its own [S19].

The signposts we will watch are concrete. A sustained move in the benchmark toward the deck's long-run path would validate the primary method and cut the value sharply; a breakdown in the RKAB approval discipline, or a repeat force majeure, would hit volume before it hit price; and any change to the royalty regime would move the cost line in a way the model would have to reflect [S0, S13]. On the other side, a decision by the board to maintain or raise the payout ratio through a price decline would be the strongest possible signal that management sees the downturn as cyclical rather than structural [S8].
The konglo profile

Bayan is a single-name group: the listed vehicle of Low Tuck Kwong, whose register is dominated by the founder and his family and, since the October transfers, by PT Jhonlin Baratama. It sits on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list, and that status takes it out of the IHSG calculation from 2 November 2026 [S23, S24] and out of the LQ45/IDX30/IDX80. HSC membership is a concentration reading and not a finding of wrongdoing, and it is not a BYAN-specific index deletion: the MSCI Standalone consultation is a class-level regime risk that would touch every HSC name, not an action already taken on this one [S19, S17]. The free float is 21.3% of the register, above the new fifteen-percent minimum, so Bayan is not a name facing a forced sell-down to comply — the flow risk for the class is real, but for Bayan the binding constraint is that so few shares trade that the marginal price is set by a thin market rather than by value [S0, S18]. The group's role is uncomplicated: Bayan is the flagship asset and the group's principal cash generator, and the corporate action that matters is the pending change of control — a conditional share purchase agreement, the PJBS the exchange referred to, which would transfer the control block to PT Jhonlin Baratama subject to conditions precedent, with the tender-offer obligation the takeover rules attach to completion [S2, S10].

The register reconciles only once the affiliate block is named. The exchange's list of holders above five percent at the end of March 2026 shows Dato' Low Tuck Kwong at 40.2% of the capital, Elaine Low at 22.0%, PT Sumber Suryadaya Prima at 10.0% and a public line of 27.8% [S5]. Sumber Suryadaya Prima is not an anonymous holder: the FY2025 accounts include it in the related-party trade-receivables note [S6, F88], so its tenth of the register sits in the non-float block, not with the public. After the October transfers the named holdings are Low at 8.3%, Elaine Low at 22.0%, Jhonlin at 30.2% and Sumber Suryadaya Prima at 10.0% — leaving a residual public line that does not fully reconcile to the registry's free-float measure of 21.3%, because the IDX-IC methodology uses a different, affiliate-adjusted definition of float than the company's public line. We state the gap rather than smooth it: the thin-float argument and the HSC flag rest on a register that the disclosures explain in outline but not to the last share [S5, S6].

Ownership and control are the governance story here, and they moved in the covered period — but the distinction that matters, and that the group registry records as 'pending' (as the red team notes), is between the SHARES having moved and CONTROL having changed. The shares moved: PT Jhonlin Baratama, which held nothing in the March 2026 shareholder list, held 30.2% of the issued and paid-up capital by the 19 October ownership report, while Dato' Low Tuck Kwong's stake fell to 8.3% [S5, S10]. Control did not: Dato' Low Tuck Kwong and Elaine Low still hold 30.3% together, marginally above Jhonlin's 30.2%, and the company states, on the basis of their 8 October 2026 control letters and the absence of any takeover announcement under POJK 9/2018, that it has received nothing showing a change of control [S10]. The 16 September 2026 conditional SPA is the agreed mechanism: it covers 10,000,000,500 shares shares and depends on conditions precedent the company did not spell out [S25], and the block transferred on its formula, but the formal change of control — and with it the mandatory tender offer — has NOT been triggered. The 19 October holding report shows Jhonlin at 10,084,088,370 shares shares, some eighty-four million more than the SPA block — under a third of one percent of the register — which the disclosure does not explain; we flag the difference rather than smooth it [S10, S25]. That is the consistent reading of the disclosure: the 30.2% holding, the exchange's clarification questions and the registry's 'not yet completed' status all describe a block that has moved without control having passed.

The disclosed transfers that prompted the exchange's questions were executed off-market at Rp2,588 a share in the middle of that October and again at Rp2,588 a share the next day, against a Rp11,100 close on the first of those days and a Rp11,200 on-market purchase by Dato' Low Tuck Kwong the day before — so the transfer price is a little under a quarter of the tape, not a "small fraction" of it [S2, S10]. Two facts discipline the reading. First, the price is contractual rather than a discovery: the exchange tied the identical first-day price directly to the pelaksanaan Perjanjian Jual Beli Saham Bersyarat (PJBS), a conditional share purchase agreement, with Jhonlin Baratama, and asked whether a change to that agreement had produced a further transfer [S2]. The buyer is PT Jhonlin Baratama and the sellers are the control-block holders, so this is a transfer between connected parties on a PJBS formula, not a minority price fixed by the market [S10]. Second, the holdings confirm it moved between existing holders rather than off the register: as at the October ownership report Dato' Low Tuck Kwong held 8.3% of the capital, he and Elaine Low together held 30.3%, and PT Jhonlin Baratama held 30.2% as the resulting stake [S2, S10]. We therefore do not claim an unsourced aggregate block; the disclosure supports the per-date prices and the resulting holdings, and no more. The company answered that it was not a party to the transactions and could not confirm their substance, and both it and the ministry denied any link to the RKAB process [S2, S10, S15].

The question this raises for an outside shareholder is about the alignment of the controlling block rather than about disclosure compliance. A transfer at a price far below the market, from or to parties connected with control, is the kind of event that makes the market ask what the transacting parties believe the shares are worth, and it coincided with the RKAB approval process, which the mining ministry publicly stressed was unrelated to the share acquisition [S15]. We note that both the company and the ministry took the trouble to deny a connection, which tells you the connection was being made [S13, S15].

On the rest of the governance file the picture is unremarkable and mostly positive. The dividend record is strong and consistent, with a five-year average payout of 73.0% and a large distribution in respect of the last completed year [S8]. The board and audit arrangements show no flagged issues in the covered filings, there is no auditor downgrade or qualified opinion, and we found no serial equity issuance or pledge disclosure that would impair control [S6]. Related-party revenue is DISCLOSED AND QUANTIFIED, not dismissed: the group's coal revenue includes US$185.9m from related parties in the last full year — a mid-single-digit share of group sales — against a smaller related-party balance-sheet footing of US$35.2m trade payables and US$12.3m trade receivables, plus a US$51.9m civil-works contract with PT Nirmala Matranusa [S6]. That is the flag the methodology requires us to quantify, and we classify it optics-class rather than manipulation-class: the flows are disclosed line by line, small against revenue and assets, and the coal is also sold to third parties — but the payable is not nothing, and it sits beside the off-market block transfer above rather than being waved away [S6].

On ESG, the exposures are the ones intrinsic to thermal coal. The group's emissions are scope one and scope two from mining, hauling and barging plus the much larger scope three from combustion of the coal it sells, and the latter is the material figure for any investor applying a transition lens [S6]. Land rehabilitation and mine-closure obligations are a real long-tail liability for any Kalimantan producer, and the group's reclamation provisioning is a line we will track through the filings [S6]. On the social side, the mining workforce is large and locally concentrated, which creates both licence-to-operate value and community-relations risk [S6]. None of this changes the investment case at the price in question, but a transition-aware buyer should size the position for the scope-three exposure rather than for the reported emissions [S6].

The nearest dated catalyst is the HSC exit from the IHSG calculation on 2 November 2026 [S23, S24]; the next fundamental one is the FY2026 full-year result and the board's dividend recommendation, which will show whether the force-majeure episode cost volume that the additional quota does not recover and whether the contracted book of 67.2 Mt is holding [S8, S13]. Alongside it sits the FY2027 RKAB cycle for the three affected subsidiaries, because an orderly approval would remove the single largest operational tail risk in the model and a repeat delay would reprice it [S13], and the 1 January 2027 move of coal exports to the state exporter, which puts an execution deadline on the export channel [S22].

The dividend decision is the value catalyst, and it is the one the market actually trades. The company's five-year record of a 73.0% payout is the anchor the multiple rests on, and a board decision to maintain or raise the payout through a weakening price would be read as a signal about management's own view of the cycle [S8]. Conversely, a cut would validate the primary valuation method faster than any price move [S0].

We will monitor a short list of indicators between updates. First, the benchmark price path against the deck's assumption, since the sensitivity grid shows it dominates every other variable [S0]. Second, the realised-price spread to the benchmark, because it is the company-specific number that tells us whether the quality discount is widening or narrowing [S6]. Third, unit cash costs against our bottom-up build, with fuel and contracting rates the inputs to watch [S8]. Fourth, the RKAB calendar and any further force-majeure disclosure [S13]. Fifth, and at the governance level, any further disclosure on the Jhonlin Baratama block and the resolution of the exchange's clarification request [S2, S10]. We will revisit the through-cycle marker itself if the complex moves, as the method card requires, rather than assuming the deck stands still [S0].

The regime calendar is now a monitored list in its own right, because on this name it sets the price as much as the coal does [S19]. The first dated item lands tomorrow: the HSC names, Bayan included, leave the IHSG calculation on 2 November 2026 [S23, S24], and we will watch whether the exit produces the passive outflow or the price resilience the base regime assumes. The next is the exchange's minimum-free-float step for the largest names at the end of March 2027 [S18]. Then MSCI's Standalone decision, with the feedback window closing at the end of April 2027 and the decision due by the end of June 2027 [S17]. The third is any completion, amendment or lapse of the Jhonlin Baratama agreement and the tender-offer process that follows it, and any further exchange or regulator clarification on the October transfers [S2, S10]. We will also track the HSC list itself, since an addition or removal changes whether the lens carries the HSC flag at all, and with it the share of the premium the most likely path keeps [S19].

bear.narrative: The war premium unwinds and overshoots: the bear takes the deck's long-run Newcastle marker down a full 20% (the exact mirror of the bull, the house default), which is a demand-led trough through the US$100-110/t marginal-cost floor the coal deck itself names, and the RKAB quota squeeze persists and clips a twentieth of group volume — the disclosed one-off cure ESDM granted the three affected subsidiaries was larger, an additional 15-20 Mt or about a fifth to a quarter of group output [S14], so the bear carries a lasting residual clip rather than the temporary halt annualised. The same mirrored volume clip also absorbs the 1 January 2027 state-exporter transition: the registered-exporter permit runs only to end-2026 and the industry association warns the handover to PT Danantara Sumberdaya Indonesia could stop cargoes at the start of the year — a working-capital and execution risk for a producer that sells most tonnes offshore [S22, review C16] — so the bear's x0.95 now carries a quarter of export disruption inside the one volume shock rather than a fifth, non-mirrored shock. On the cost side the IUP/CCOW conversion risk crystallises and the effective royalty steps up toward the top IUP rate — a +3.5pp move on the royalty line. The new Jhonlin control block is carried as a separate +200bp governance overhang on the required return rather than as a price move, and the lower benchmark with the unchanged 73% payout cuts the dividend mechanically — so the bear value and the dividend cut arrive together, because the dividend is the anchor the market pays for.

bull.narrative: The mirror of the bear on the same four drivers, with each easing capped by a hard policy or peer floor rather than left open (round-1 review C4). The war premium holds and Chinese mine-safety curbs plus Indonesian supply discipline keep seaborne supply tight into 2027: the annual report records a national production cap of approximately 600 Mt against the 2025 target of 790 Mt, about a quarter lower [S6 p.74, F81, F82], which is the domestic supply leg the deck's tightness story rests on, and the benchmark HOLDS NEAR THE DECK'S REVIEWED SPOT — about 27% above the FY2027E path, above the plain +20% mirror — because the deck's own reviewed spot of US$150.35/t sits there and a spot-persists regime is the most obvious upside for the long case (review C19). Bayan's low-cost Tabang tonnes take share and volumes run 5% above the base plan as the Muara Pahu and Tabang capacity, funded by the US$0.77bn of debottlenecking capex already spent, runs full — the base already sits at the company's more-than-80-million-MT-per-annum ramp target [S6, F33], so the bullish volume leg is the mirror of the bear's clip rather than a second step up. Royalty is eased only to the IUP schedule's 6% floor [S6, F30], a 2pp move from the 8% the LK pays, because no policy in the file produces a sub-6% rate and the 7.9% effective expense (F26) sits above that floor. The required return falls by the base's own +100bp governance charge and no further, landing at 10.3% — above the lowest covered coal peer's cost of equity (10.29%) — as the control question resolves: whether the Jhonlin process completes into a tender or lapses, either outcome ends the POJK 9/2018 uncertainty the company itself flagged in its 23 Oct 2026 disclosure [S10]. The bear's +200bp is therefore larger than the bull's -100bp, and deliberately so: the bull cannot price a country-risk-free cost of equity or a royalty below the IUP floor.
